query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coating tungsten particles with a thin, vapor‐deposited nickel interlayer prior to spark plasma sintering with copper will enhance the wetting and bonding between the W and Cu phases, thus reducing void formation and phase separation and improving thermal transport and mechanical durability for fusion‐reactor heat-transfer joints compared to conventional SPS processing.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or interconnected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix, as produced by typical powder metallurgy routes (e.g., SPS) that currently show phase separation, voids, and nonuniform interfacial contact.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers) Ni coating onto W particles via vapor deposition before mixing with Cu powder and consolidating the mix by spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: The process is conducted in an inert atmosphere using SPS at temperatures kept below the boiling point of Cu; service conditions include exposure to high thermal flux and irradiation typical of fusion reactor joint environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni interlayer serves as a wetting enhancer and diffusion mediator, forming a graded interface between W and Cu that minimizes interfacial energy mismatches and void formation during rapid sintering.
generation.mechanism: Nickel exhibits good wettability and solubility with both tungsten and copper. Its presence promotes liquid-phase bonding of copper around tungsten particles during SPS, thereby enabling near-complete densification and a defect-free interface. This improved interfacial integrity is expected to sustain high thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline SPS-processed W–Cu composite without a Ni interlayer, the Ni-coated W–Cu composite will show reduced porosity, enhanced interfacial uniformity, improved thermal conductivity, and sustained mechanical strength under fusion reactor irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as SPS of mixed W and Cu powders without any interfacial modification (or interlayer coating), which have been shown to suffer from voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: Processing is confined to the temperature regime that avoids Cu boiling and oxidation (SPS temperatures below ~1000°C) and service conditions mimicking high-flux, irradiative fusion reactor joints; long-term stability of the Ni interlayer under these conditions remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Ni coating thickness and uniformity, as well as the potential for unwanted intermetallic formation or diffusion over prolonged high-temperature irradiation exposure, require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites using SPS: one using vapor-deposited Ni-coated W particles and a control set with uncoated W particles. Characterize the microstructure (porosity and interfacial bonding) using SEM/TEM, measure thermal conductivity, and subject samples to simulated irradiation conditions relevant to fusion environments.
measurements: Porosity and void analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Interfacial microstructure characterization via transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Mechanical testing (e.g., compressive yield strength) before and after irradiation simulations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composite does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in void content, improved interfacial bonding, and enhanced thermal and mechanical performance under irradiation compared to the uncoated control, the hypothesis is falsified.
